question.text: 30-Day and 1-year mortality in emergency general surgery laparotomies: an area of concern and need for improvement?
question.context: Emergency surgery is associated with poorer outcomes and higher mortality with recent studies suggesting the 30-day mortality to be 14-15%. The aim of this study was to analyse the 30-day mortality, age-related 30-day mortality and 1-year mortality following emergency laparotomy. We hope this will encourage prospective data collection, improvement of care and initiate strategies to establish best practice in this area. This was a retrospective study of patients who underwent emergency laparotomy from June 2010 to May 2012. The primary end point of the study was 30-day mortality, age-related 30-day mortality and 1-year all-cause mortality. 477 laparotomies were performed in 446 patients. 57% were aged<70 and 43% aged>70 years. 30-day mortality was 12, 4% in those aged<70 years and 22% in those>70 years (p<0.001). 1-year mortality was 25, 15% in those aged under 70 years and 38% in those aged>70 years (p<0.001).

medgemma_4b.clinical_reasoning: The study clearly demonstrates a significant increase in 30-day and 1-year mortality rates in patients aged >70 years compared to those aged <70 years undergoing emergency laparotomy. This difference is statistically significant (p<0.001). Therefore, it is reasonable to conclude that the mortality rate is an area of concern and needs improvement.
medgemma_4b.critical_evidence: 30-day mortality was 12, 4% in those aged<70 years and 22% in those>70 years (p<0.001). 1-year mortality was 25, 15% in those aged under 70 years and 38% in those aged>70 years (p<0.001).
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: While other factors could contribute to mortality, the age-related difference in mortality is a strong indicator that age is a significant risk factor in this population. Other potential confounders, such as comorbidities, were not explicitly addressed in the study, but the age-related difference is the most direct and compelling finding.

rnj1_8b.clinical_reasoning: The study shows higher 30-day and 1-year mortality in emergency laparotomies, particularly in patients over 70 years. The data supports the need for improvement in emergency surgery outcomes, making option A (yes) the best choice.
rnj1_8b.critical_evidence: 30-day mortality was 12% in those under 70 and 22% in those over 70 (p<0.001), indicating a significant age-related mortality difference.
rnj1_8b.differential_considered: No differential diagnoses needed as this is a descriptive study analyzing outcomes, not a patient with specific symptoms requiring diagnosis.

qwen3_vl_8b.clinical_reasoning: The study demonstrates significantly higher 30-day and 1-year mortality in patients aged >70 years compared to those <70 years, indicating a clear area of concern and need for improvement in emergency laparotomy outcomes. The data supports targeted interventions to reduce mortality in this high-risk group.
qwen3_vl_8b.critical_evidence: 30-day mortality was 22% in patients >70 years vs. 12.4% in those <70 years (p<0.001), and 1-year mortality was 38% vs. 25.15% (p<0.001), highlighting a substantial disparity.
qwen3_vl_8b.differential_considered: No differential diagnoses were applicable as this is a retrospective epidemiological study focused on mortality outcomes, not a diagnostic case. The key consideration was whether the findings indicate a need for improvement, which they clearly do.

olmo3_7b.differential_considered: Other possible differentials (e.g., comorbidities, preoperative status) were likely considered but are less directly supported by the provided data than the age-related mortality trends, which are clearly and significantly worse in the older group.
